title: Sister Death
hook: Francis, near the end of his life, adds a verse to his Canticle of the Creatures praising Sister Death

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's taunt: O death, where is thy sting? Your line was where is thy sting. Which sentence did you read slowly? Paul called death an enemy. Today, a saint calls it family. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

Brother Sun. Sister Moon and the stars. Brother Wind. Sister Water. Brother Fire. Mother Earth. These are the names in a song by Francis of Assisi, written in the everyday Italian of his region rather than in church Latin. It's called the Canticle of the Creatures, or the Canticle of the Sun, and it praises God for each of them, one at a time, as if the whole world were a household. Tradition says that near the end of his life, sick and nearly blind, Francis added one more name to the family.
screen: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.` → `A SONG OF THE WHOLE HOUSEHOLD.` → `ONE MORE NAME, NEAR THE END.`

segments.voice: First, a family. Francis doesn't praise the sun as a lamp or water as a resource. He gives each a place at the table. Sister Water is useful and humble and precious and pure. Brother Fire is beautiful and strong. Everything in the song is kin. Second, one more sister. The new verse praises God for our Sister Bodily Death, from whom no living person can escape. Read that slowly. Francis doesn't say death is pleasant, or optional, or not real. He says it is certain. And then he calls it sister, the same word he used for the moon. Third, not a shrug. The verse goes on, and it isn't sentimental. It warns: woe to those who die in mortal sin. And it calls blessed those whom death finds doing God's holy will, for the second death will do them no harm. Some readers hear in that phrase an echo of the book of Revelation. For Francis, a sister can still be serious. Fourth, the difference a name makes. An enemy is something you fight. A sister is someone who comes, whether you are ready or not, but who belongs to the household. Yesterday Paul called death the last enemy. Today Francis calls it sister. Both words come from Christian voices. Death is the same in both. What changes is where it sits: outside the door, or at the table. Sister death.
screen: `EVERY CREATURE IS KIN.` · `OUR SISTER BODILY DEATH.` · `SERIOUS, NOT SENTIMENTAL.` · `AN ENEMY, OR A SISTER.` · then, large: `SISTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Settle and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one ending in your life that has already happened: a school year, a job, a move, a friendship that ran its course, a habit you finally put down. Not a raw loss, if that's too much today. A finished thing. Look at what it made room for. Then, in your own words or just with attention, thank it. Thank the ending as if it had been a sister walking you to a door. If you pray, you can offer that thanks to God, as Francis did. The bell holds the time.
Sister Death: Francis of Assisi's name for bodily death in his Canticle of the Creatures, certain and unavoidable, and still counted as family. Today's word.
Your line: sister death. Today, when something ends, even something small like a day's work, give it a nod before you move on. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Franciscans and other Christians sing or pray the Canticle of the Creatures, and in Franciscan communities the death of a brother or sister is sometimes spoken of as the coming of Sister Death.

notes: The Canticle is paraphrased throughout; no pre-1929 English translation quoted. Confirm the epithets: Water 'useful, humble, precious, pure'; Fire 'bright and strong' (the original also has 'jocund' / joyful and 'robust'); Death 'from whom no living person can escape'.

'Tradition says that near the end of his life, sick and nearly blind, Francis added one more name': this follows the early lives (Celano, Legend of Perugia). The index hook's year (1226) is left out under the claims rule.
Original left null: the Umbrian phrase 'sora nostra Morte corporale' could be added if a Keeper confirms the spelling (the validator flags plain-ASCII originals).
'Both words come from Christian voices' pairs Paul (day 778) and Francis without ranking them.
howItsDone: confirm the Franciscan usage of 'Sister Death'.
Audit: cut 'an enemy is something you fight until you lose', which quietly contradicted Paul's claim from day 778 that death is the enemy that loses.
Editor: Fire's epithet changed from 'bright' to 'beautiful' (closer to the Umbrian 'bello'); the mortal-sin line now reads as a warning ('woe', 'guai') rather than grief, in the teach and the myth.
